name: Pharaoh Hophra
interpretive_note: Jeremiah 44:30 is the only verse that names this king. The other passages here speak of an unnamed "Pharaoh" but are set in the same years -- Zedekiah's rebellion, the siege and fall of Jerusalem, and the flight to Egypt that followed -- which is why they are usually identified with Hophra (called Apries by Greek historians, reigned c. 589-570 BC). Jeremiah 46:13-26 is undated; its remark that Pharaoh let "the appointed time" pass (46:17) is often read as a play on Hophra's name. Ezekiel 29:17-21, dated some sixteen years after the fall of Jerusalem, may fall at the very end of his reign or under his successor. The earlier Pharaoh Neco, whom Jeremiah 46:2 names, has his own entry.
source_summary: Hophra (Apries), king of Egypt in Judah's last years, whose army briefly drew the Babylonians away from besieged Jerusalem, and against whom Jeremiah and Ezekiel pronounced judgment; Jeremiah foretold that he would be handed over to his enemies (Jeremiah 44:30).
family_friendly_summary: Pharaoh Hophra was the king of Egypt during the last years of the kingdom of Judah. Judah's king Zedekiah hoped Egypt would save Jerusalem from the Babylonian army. When Pharaoh's army marched out, the Babylonians left for a while, but the prophet Jeremiah warned that they would come back -- and they did, and Jerusalem fell. The prophet Ezekiel compared this proud king to a great river monster and to a tall cedar tree that God would cut down. Later, Jeremiah said by name that God would hand Pharaoh Hophra over to his enemies. These messages warned God's people not to trust a powerful nation instead of trusting the LORD.
adult_story: Pharaoh Hophra ruled Egypt when Judah's last king, Zedekiah, rebelled against Babylon and looked to Egypt for horses and troops (Ezekiel 17:15-17). While Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem, Pharaoh's army marched out of Egypt and the Babylonians withdrew. Zedekiah's court took hope, but Jeremiah warned that the Egyptian army would go home and the Babylonians would return and burn the city -- and so it happened (Jeremiah 37:5-11). Ezekiel, among the exiles in Babylon, prophesied against the same Pharaoh in a series of dated oracles: God would drag Egypt's king like a great monster out of his Nile (Ezekiel 29:2-3), break his arms so he could not hold a sword (30:21-25), and cut him down like a towering cedar that fell because its heart was proud (31:2-18); Ezekiel then raised a lament over him going down to the pit with the fallen nations (32:2-32). After Jerusalem fell, a remnant of Judah fled to Egypt against the LORD's word. At Tahpanhes, where Pharaoh had a palace, Jeremiah buried large stones and declared that Nebuchadnezzar would set his throne over them (Jeremiah 43:9-10). Then he named the king: the LORD would give Pharaoh Hophra into the hand of his enemies, just as He had given Zedekiah into Nebuchadnezzar's hand (44:30). Judah had trusted Egypt to rescue it; the prophets warned that Egypt's king could not even save himself.

devotionals: Judah trusted Pharaoh's army to save Jerusalem, but it turned back and the city fell, just as Jeremiah said. Jesus is the only rescuer who never retreats when we need Him.

name_meaning.meaning: Pharaoh, "great house" (a royal title, not a personal name); Hophra, from the Egyptian Wahibre, "constant is the heart of Ra"
